title: Ἀνδράγρια
about: Hector, carried to the river Xanthus, is laid on the ground and washed with water; he revives, vomits blood, and falls back unconscious. Seeing him gone, the Argives press the Trojans harder. Ajax son of Oileus kills Satnius; Polydamas avenges him by wounding Prothoenor and vaunts over him. Telamonian Ajax casts at Polydamas, misses, and kills Antenor’s son Archelochus instead, and points out the likeness to Antenor. Acamas kills Promachus over his brother and boasts; Peneleos kills Ilioneus, strikes off his head and holds it up as a message to the Trojans, who tremble. The poet calls on the Muses to name the first Achaean to win spoils after Poseidon turned the battle, and lists the kills; Ajax son of Oileus takes the most, being the best at pursuing men in flight.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ πόρον ἷξον ἐϋρρεῖος ποταμοῖο
Ξάνθου δινήεντος, ὃν ἀθάνατος τέκετο Ζεύς,
ἔνθά μιν ἐξ ἵππων πέλασαν χθονί, κὰδ δέ οἱ ὕδωρ
χεῦαν·
sentences.l:
But when now the ford they reached of the fair-flowing river,
of eddying Xanthus, whom immortal Zeus begot,
there him from the horses they brought near to the ground, and down on him water
poured;
sentences.i: But when they came to the ford of the fair-flowing river, eddying Xanthus, whom immortal Zeus begot, they took him down from the horses and laid him on the ground, and poured water over him.
sentences.n: Hector’s companions, who were carrying him out of the fight at the end of the last part, reach the river. ἷξον is the unaugmented aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’, πόρον is ‘ford’, and ἐϋρρεῖος is the epic genitive of ἐϋρρεής ‘fair-flowing’. Ξάνθου δινήεντος ‘of eddying Xanthus’ names the river, and ὃν … τέκετο ‘whom … begot’ is said of a father: the river is a god’s son. μιν is Hector; ἐξ ἵππων ‘from the horses’ means from the chariot; πέλασαν is the aorist of πελάζω ‘bring near’. κὰδ … χεῦαν is ‘poured down’, the preverb split from its verb. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 436.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀμπνύνθη καὶ ἀνέδρακεν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν,
ἑζόμενος δ’ ἐπὶ γοῦνα κελαινεφὲς αἷμ’ ἀπέμεσσεν·
sentences.l:
and he recovered breath and looked up with his eyes,
and sitting on his knees dark-clouded blood he vomited up;
sentences.i: He drew breath again and looked up, and, sitting on his knees, vomited blood dark as a cloud.
sentences.n: Hector comes round. ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’, a pronoun. ἀμπνύνθη, ‘recovered breath’, is the aorist passive of ἀμπνύω, a form of ἀναπνέω ‘breathe again’; ἀνέδρακεν is the aorist of ἀναδέρκομαι ‘look up’, and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is an epic dative plural. ἑζόμενος ‘sitting’ goes with ἐπὶ γοῦνα ‘onto his knees’: he is kneeling or sitting back on them. κελαινεφὲς αἷμ’ is the stock ‘dark-clouded blood’, and ἀπέμεσσεν is the aorist of ἀπεμέω ‘vomit up’. The unit begins mid-line, after the stop.

sentences.t:
αὖτις δ’ ἐξοπίσω πλῆτο χθονί, τὼ δέ οἱ ὄσσε
νὺξ ἐκάλυψε μέλαινα·
sentences.l:
And again to the rear he came near to the ground, and for him the two eyes
night covered, black;
sentences.i: Then he sank back to the ground again, and black night covered his eyes;
sentences.n: He collapses a second time. αὖτις is ‘again’ and ἐξοπίσω ‘to the rear’. πλῆτο is an unaugmented aorist that belongs with πελάζω ‘bring near’, the verb of πέλασαν in 435: they brought him near the ground, and now he comes near it again by falling. τὼ … ὄσσε is ‘the two eyes’, a dual noun with the dual article, and οἱ ‘for him’ says whose. νὺξ … μέλαινα is ‘black night’, the Greek for a faint, and ἐκάλυψε ‘covered’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 439.

sentences.t: βέλος δ’ ἔτι θυμὸν ἐδάμνα.
sentences.l: and the missile still was subduing his spirit.
sentences.i: and the missile was still overcoming his spirit.
sentences.n: Why he is not yet well. βέλος is any thrown missile; the house rendering is ‘shaft’ for arrows and spears, but here it is the stone that struck him, so ‘missile’ is used. ἔτι is ‘still’, θυμόν ‘spirit’, and ἐδάμνα the imperfect of δαμνάω ‘subdue’: the blow was still working on him. The unit begins mid-line, after the stop.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ὡς οὖν ἴδον Ἕκτορα νόσφι κιόντα
μᾶλλον ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι θόρον, μνήσαντο δὲ χάρμης.
sentences.l:
And the Argives, when then they saw Hector going apart,
the more upon the Trojans leapt, and remembered the joy of battle.
sentences.i: And when the Argives saw Hector going away, they leapt the more upon the Trojans and remembered the joy of battle.
sentences.n: The Argives take heart as Hector is led off. ὡς οὖν ἴδον is ‘when then they saw’, ἴδον an unaugmented aorist, and νόσφι κιόντα is ‘going apart’, the participle of κίω ‘go’. θόρον ‘leapt’ is the aorist of θρῴσκω, and μᾶλλον ‘the more’ goes with it. μνήσαντο δὲ χάρμης ‘remembered the joy of battle’ takes the genitive, χάρμη being the joy of fighting. Line 441 is the same line as 8.252, with the same English.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα πολὺ πρώτιστος Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας
Σάτνιον οὔτασε δουρὶ μετάλμενος ὀξυόεντι
Ἠνοπίδην, ὃν ἄρα νύμφη τέκε νηῒς ἀμύμων
Ἤνοπι βουκολέοντι παρ’ ὄχθας Σατνιόεντος.
sentences.l:
There by far the first, of Oileus the swift Ajax
Satnius wounded with a spear, leaping on him, a sharp one,
Enops’-son, whom then a nymph bore, a Naiad, blameless,
to Enops, as he tended cattle, by the banks of Satnioeis.
sentences.i: There swift Ajax, son of Oileus, was by far the first: he leapt on Satnius, the son of Enops, and stabbed him with his sharp spear. A blameless Naiad nymph had borne him to Enops, while Enops tended cattle by the banks of the Satnioeis.
sentences.n: This is Ajax son of Oileus, the lesser Ajax; Telamonian Ajax is named at 459. ἔνθα … πολὺ πρώτιστος is ‘there, by far the first’, πολύ strengthening the superlative. Σάτνιον is the victim and Ἠνοπίδην ‘Enops’-son’ a patronymic in apposition. οὔτασε is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound by a thrust’, μετάλμενος ‘leaping on’, and ὀξυόεντι ‘sharp’. In the relative clause νύμφη … νηῒς is a Naiad, ἀμύμων ‘blameless’ (its sense is not known), and ὄχθας Σατνιόεντος ‘the banks of the Satnioeis’ shows a river.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν Ὀϊλιάδης δουρὶ κλυτὸς ἐγγύθεν ἐλθὼν
οὖτα κατὰ λαπάρην·
sentences.l:
Him, Oileus’-son, famous with the spear, having come close,
wounded in the flank;
sentences.i: The son of Oileus, famous with the spear, came close and stabbed him in the flank;
sentences.n: The same Ajax, named now by his patronymic Ὀϊλιάδης ‘Oileus’-son’, finishes Satnius. τὸν μέν ‘him’ is Satnius. δουρὶ κλυτός ‘famous with the spear’ is a stock epithet, and ἐγγύθεν ἐλθών ‘coming close’ is a half-line that returns. οὖτα, ‘wounded’, is a shorter form of the verb of οὔτασε in 443. κατὰ λαπάρην is ‘in the flank’, the soft part below the ribs. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 447.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀνετράπετ’, ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτῷ
Τρῶες καὶ Δαναοὶ σύναγον κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην.
sentences.l:
and he was overturned, and around him then
Trojans and Danaans brought together strong battle.
sentences.i: and he fell over backwards, and around him Trojans and Danaans joined in strong battle.
sentences.n: Satnius falls and the fight closes round him. ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’. ἀνετράπετ’ is the aorist of ἀνατρέπω ‘overturn’, here ‘was knocked over’, with its final vowel elided. ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ αὐτῷ is ‘around him then’, the preposition coming before its pronoun with the particles between. σύναγον ‘brought together’ is a past tense without the augment, and κρατερὴν ὑσμίνην is ‘strong battle’. Δαναοί is the second of the three names for the Achaeans. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἐπὶ Πουλυδάμας ἐγχέσπαλος ἦλθεν ἀμύντωρ
Πανθοΐδης, βάλε δὲ Προθοήνορα δεξιὸν ὦμον
υἱὸν Ἀρηϊλύκοιο, δι’ ὤμου δ’ ὄβριμον ἔγχος
ἔσχεν, ὃ δ’ ἐν κονίῃσι πεσὼν ἕλε γαῖαν ἀγοστῷ.
sentences.l:
And to him came up Polydamas, spear-brandishing, a defender,
Panthous’-son, and hit Prothoenor on the right shoulder,
son of Areilycus, and through the shoulder the mighty spear
held, and he, in the dust having fallen, took the earth in the crook of his arm.
sentences.i: Polydamas, the spear-brandishing son of Panthous, came up as a defender to where he lay, and hit Prothoenor on the right shoulder, the son of Areilycus; the mighty spear held fast through the shoulder, and he fell in the dust and clutched the earth in the crook of his arm.
sentences.n: A Trojan counter-stroke. τῷ δ’ ἐπί is ‘to him’, to Satnius, and ἀμύντωρ ‘defender’ (from ἀμύνω ‘ward off’) gives the reason Polydamas comes. ἐγχέσπαλος ‘spear-brandishing’ is the table’s epithet (its formation is uncertain); Πανθοΐδης is the patronymic ‘Panthous’-son’. βάλε … Προθοήνορα δεξιὸν ὦμον puts the man and the part struck both in the accusative; υἱὸν Ἀρηϊλύκοιο is ‘son of Areilycus’. ἔσχεν, the aorist of ἔχω, is ‘held’, the spear stuck fast. In the last line ἀγοστῷ is a rare noun whose sense is not known; ‘the crook of the arm’ is the usual guess. The unit runs four lines to the first full stop.

sentences.t: Πουλυδάμας δ’ ἔκπαγλον ἐπεύξατο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.l: And Polydamas terribly vaunted, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And Polydamas cried out terribly in triumph, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: Polydamas boasts over the man he has hit. ἐπεύξατο is the aorist of ἐπεύχομαι ‘vaunt’, ἔκπαγλον an adverbial accusative ‘terribly’, and μακρὸν ἀΰσας ‘shouting loudly’, the aorist participle of ἀΰω ‘shout’. The whole line is a speech introduction, and it returns at 478 with Acamas’ name.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὰν αὖτ’ ὀΐω μεγαθύμου Πανθοΐδαο
χειρὸς ἄπο στιβαρῆς ἅλιον πηδῆσαι ἄκοντα,
ἀλλά τις Ἀργείων κόμισε χροΐ, καί μιν ὀΐω
αὐτῷ σκηπτόμενον κατίμεν δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω.
sentences.l:
“Surely not, in turn, do I think, of great-hearted Panthous’-son
from the stout hand has it leapt in vain, the javelin,
but some one of the Argives received it in his flesh, and him I think
on it leaning to go down into the house of Hades.”
sentences.i: “I do not think, this time, that the javelin has leapt in vain from the stout hand of great-hearted Panthous’ son; some one of the Argives has received it in his flesh, and I think he is going down into the house of Hades, leaning on it.”
sentences.n: Polydamas speaks of himself in the third person, ‘Panthous’ son’ (the epic genitive Πανθοΐδαο). οὐ μὰν αὖτ’ ὀΐω ‘surely not this time, I think’ takes an infinitive: ἅλιον πηδῆσαι ἄκοντα ‘that the javelin leapt in vain’, with χειρὸς ἄπο στιβαρῆς ‘from the stout hand’. κόμισε, ‘received’, has an Argive as subject, and χροΐ is ‘in his flesh’. He means the dying Prothoenor. καί μιν ὀΐω is a second ‘I think’; κατίμεν = κατιέναι ‘to go down’, and αὐτῷ σκηπτόμενον ‘leaning on it’ makes the spear his staff on the way to δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω ‘into the house of Hades’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀργείοισι δ’ ἄχος γένετ’ εὐξαμένοιο·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and for the Argives grief arose, as he declared it aloud;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and grief came upon the Argives as he declared it aloud;
sentences.n: The Argives’ reaction to the boast. ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech, ἄχος γένετ’ is ‘grief arose’ with Ἀργείοισι ‘for the Argives’, and εὐξαμένοιο is a genitive absolute, ‘as he declared it aloud’. The line is the same as 13.417, with the same English. The edition ends it at an ano teleia, so the sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t:
Αἴαντι δὲ μάλιστα δαΐφρονι θυμὸν ὄρινε
τῷ Τελαμωνιάδῃ·
sentences.l:
and for Ajax most of all, wise-minded, it stirred the heart,
him, Telamon’s-son;
sentences.i: and it stirred most of all the heart of Ajax, the son of Telamon, wise-hearted as he was;
sentences.n: The grief reaches Telamonian Ajax. Αἴαντι … θυμὸν ὄρινε is ‘stirred Ajax’s heart’, ὄρινε an unaugmented past tense of ὀρίνω ‘stir’, and μάλιστα ‘most of all’. δαΐφρονι is the stock ‘wise-minded’ (‘wise-hearted’ in the idiomatic English); whether it means ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed. Τελαμωνιάδῃ ‘Telamon’s-son’ is a patronymic in apposition and tells him from Oileus’ son. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 460.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ πέσεν ἄγχι μάλιστα.
sentences.l: for near him he fell, most of all.
sentences.i: for it was nearest to him that Prothoenor had fallen.
sentences.n: Why Ajax feels it most. τοῦ is Ajax in the genitive, governed by ἄγχι ‘near’; πέσεν is the unaugmented aorist of πίπτω ‘fell’, and its unnamed subject is Prothoenor. μάλιστα is ‘most’, the same word as in the line before, here ‘nearest’ with ἄγχι. γάρ gives the reason. The unit begins mid-line, after the stop.

sentences.t: καρπαλίμως δ’ ἀπιόντος ἀκόντισε δουρὶ φαεινῷ.
sentences.l: And swiftly, as he went away, he cast with a shining spear.
sentences.i: And he cast his shining spear at Polydamas as he went swiftly away.
sentences.n: Ajax answers at once. Ajax is the subject, and the target is the unstated Polydamas, put in the genitive: ἀπιόντος is ‘as he went away’, the participle of ἄπειμι, agreeing with him. καρπαλίμως ‘swiftly’ fits the moving target, and δουρὶ φαεινῷ is ‘with a shining spear’, a dative of means. The aorist ἀκόντισε comes from ἄκων ‘javelin’.

sentences.t:
Πουλυδάμας δ’ αὐτὸς μὲν ἀλεύατο κῆρα μέλαιναν
λικριφὶς ἀΐξας, κόμισεν δ’ Ἀντήνορος υἱὸς
Ἀρχέλοχος·
sentences.i: Polydamas himself darted aslant and avoided the black spirit of death, and it was Antenor’s son, Archelochus, who received it;
sentences.n: Polydamas dodges, and the spear finds another man. ἀλεύατο is the aorist of ἀλέομαι ‘avoid’, and κῆρα μέλαιναν is the black death-fate. λικριφίς ‘aslant’ is a rare adverb, and ἀΐξας ‘darting’ is the aorist participle of ἀΐσσω. κόμισεν, ‘received’, is the verb Polydamas used at 456, and its object is the spear, left unsaid. Ἀντήνορος υἱός ‘Antenor’s son’ is then named, Ἀρχέλοχος. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 464.

sentences.t: τῷ γάρ ῥα θεοὶ βούλευσαν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.l: for to him indeed the gods planned destruction.
sentences.i: for the gods had planned destruction for him.
sentences.n: The reason the spear found him. τῷ ‘to him’ is Archelochus, a dative of interest, and γάρ ῥα ‘for indeed’ gives the cause. βούλευσαν is the aorist of βουλεύω ‘plan’, and ὄλεθρον ‘destruction’ is its object. The unit begins mid-line, after the stop.

sentences.t:
τόν ῥ’ ἔβαλεν κεφαλῆς τε καὶ αὐχένος ἐν συνεοχμῷ,
νείατον ἀστράγαλον, ἀπὸ δ’ ἄμφω κέρσε τένοντε·
sentences.l:
Him he hit at the joining of the head and neck,
the lowest vertebra, and both tendons he cut off;
sentences.i: Ajax hit him where the head and neck join, on the lowest vertebra, and cut through both tendons.
sentences.n: Ajax’s spear strikes Archelochus. τόν ῥ’ ἔβαλεν is ‘him then he hit’; the subject, Ajax, is not named. κεφαλῆς τε καὶ αὐχένος ἐν συνεοχμῷ is ‘at the joining of head and neck’, συνεοχμός being a rare noun for a joint. νείατον ἀστράγαλον ‘the lowest vertebra’ says which, and ἀπὸ δ’ ἄμφω κέρσε τένοντε ‘cut off both tendons’ has the verb split from its preverb; κέρσε is the aorist of κείρω and τένοντε a dual.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δὲ πολὺ προτέρη κεφαλὴ στόμα τε ῥῖνές τε
οὔδεϊ πλῆντ’ ἤ περ κνῆμαι καὶ γοῦνα πεσόντος.
sentences.l:
And of him, much sooner, the head and mouth and nostrils
came near the ground than the shins and knees, as he fell.
sentences.i: As he fell, his head, mouth and nostrils came to the ground much sooner than his shins and knees.
sentences.n: Archelochus pitches forward on his face. τοῦ … πεσόντος is a genitive absolute, ‘he having fallen’. πολὺ προτέρη is ‘much earlier’; the adjective agrees with κεφαλή alone, but the plural verb πλῆντ’ takes in κεφαλή, στόμα and ῥῖνες. πλῆντ’ is the unaugmented aorist belonging with πελάζω ‘bring near’ (as in 438), and οὔδεϊ ‘to the ground’ is the epic dative of οὖδας. ἤ περ is ‘than’, and κνῆμαι are ‘shins’.

sentences.t: Αἴας δ’ αὖτ’ ἐγέγωνεν ἀμύμονι Πουλυδάμαντι·
sentences.l: And Ajax in turn called aloud to blameless Polydamas:
sentences.i: And Ajax in turn called out to blameless Polydamas:
sentences.n: Telamonian Ajax speaks to Polydamas, who has just escaped his cast. δ’ αὖτ’ is ‘and in turn’. ἐγέγωνεν is a form of the old perfect of γεγωνέω, ‘call so as to be heard’, used here as a past tense, and the dative ἀμύμονι Πουλυδάμαντι is ‘to blameless Polydamas’ (ἀμύμων is the stock ‘blameless’, whose sense is not known). The speech follows at once.

sentences.l:
“Consider, Polydamas, and to me unerringly tell:
Is not this man, for Prothoenor in return to have been slain,
worthy?
sentences.i: “Consider, Polydamas, and tell me truly: is not this man worthy to have been slain in return for Prothoenor?
sentences.n: Ajax turns Polydamas’ boast on him. φράζεο is the imperative of φράζομαι, here ‘consider’, and νημερτές, ‘unerringly’, is an adverb with ἐνίσπες, the aorist imperative of ἐνέπω ‘tell’. The question opens with ἦ ῥ’ οὐχ ‘is it not so that’, with οὗτος ἀνήρ ‘this man’ pointing at the dead Archelochus. ἀντὶ πεφάσθαι is ‘in return to have been slain’, πεφάσθαι the perfect passive infinitive of the verb of killing, with Προθοήνορος as the price paid. The Greek question mark falls in mid-line 472.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν μοι κακὸς εἴδεται οὐδὲ κακῶν ἔξ,
ἀλλὰ κασίγνητος Ἀντήνορος ἱπποδάμοιο
ἢ πάϊς·
sentences.i: He does not look to me a base man, or one of base stock, but a brother of Antenor, tamer of horses, or a son of his;
sentences.n: Ajax gives his reason. οὐ μέν μοι κακὸς εἴδεται ‘he does not seem base to me’ uses εἴδομαι ‘seem’, and οὐδὲ κακῶν ἔξ is ‘nor from base ones’ (ἔξ = ἐξ, ‘of base parents’). The next clause supplies the same verb: ἀλλὰ κασίγνητος … ἢ πάϊς, ‘but he looks a brother or a son’, with Ἀντήνορος ἱπποδάμοιο ‘of Antenor, tamer of horses’ (epic genitive in -οιο). The guess is right: Archelochus is Antenor’s son (463–464). The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 474.

sentences.t: αὐτῷ γὰρ γενεὴν ἄγχιστα ἐῴκει.
sentences.l: for to him in lineage he most nearly resembled.”
sentences.i: for in lineage he most nearly resembled him.”
sentences.n: The ground of the guess. αὐτῷ is Antenor in the dative, ‘to him’ (like him); γενεήν is an accusative of respect, ‘in lineage’, and ἄγχιστα is ‘most nearly’. ἐῴκει is the pluperfect of ἔοικα ‘resemble’, a past in sense, which says how he looked as he lay there. The unit ends Ajax’s speech, and begins mid-line, after the stop.

sentences.t: ἦ ῥ’ εὖ γιγνώσκων, Τρῶας δ’ ἄχος ἔλλαβε θυμόν.
sentences.l: He spoke, well knowing, and the Trojans grief seized in the heart.
sentences.i: So he said, knowing it well, and grief seized the Trojans in their hearts.
sentences.n: The Trojans’ reaction to Ajax’s words. ἦ is the old ‘he said’ (the imperfect of ἠμί), with ῥ’ for ῥα; it closes the speech. εὖ γιγνώσκων is ‘knowing well’, and the Greek gives no object: Ajax knew exactly who the dead man was. ἄχος ἔλλαβε ‘grief seized’ has ἔλλαβε for ἔλαβε, the doubled λ serving the metre, and Τρῶας … θυμόν puts the people and the part affected both in the accusative.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Ἀκάμας Πρόμαχον Βοιώτιον οὔτασε δουρὶ
ἀμφὶ κασιγνήτῳ βεβαώς·
sentences.l:
There Acamas wounded Promachus the Boeotian with a spear,
having stood over his brother;
sentences.i: There Acamas stabbed Promachus the Boeotian with his spear, as he stood over his brother;
sentences.n: Acamas now fights over his dead brother. ἔνθ’ is ‘there’; Πρόμαχον Βοιώτιον is ‘Promachus the Boeotian’, and οὔτασε ‘wounded’. ἀμφὶ κασιγνήτῳ βεβαώς is ‘standing over his brother’: βεβαώς is the perfect participle of βαίνω, a state, and ἀμφί with the dative means round or over. The brother is the corpse of the next unit, and 483 shows that he is the man avenged. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 477.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ὕφελκε ποδοῖιν.
sentences.l: and he was dragging him by the two feet.
sentences.i: while Promachus was dragging the body off by the feet.
sentences.n: What Promachus was doing. ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’, Promachus. ὕφελκε is the imperfect of ὑφέλκω ‘drag away’, and the unstated object is the dead man, Acamas’ brother. ποδοῖιν is the dual dative of πούς, ‘by the two feet’. The unit begins mid-line, after the stop.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ Ἀκάμας ἔκπαγλον ἐπεύξατο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.l: And over him Acamas terribly vaunted, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And Acamas cried out terribly in triumph over him, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: Acamas boasts over Promachus; τῷ is the dative ‘over him’ with ἐπεύξατο. The line is the same speech introduction as 453, with the name changed: ἔκπαγλον ‘terribly’ and μακρὸν ἀΰσας ‘shouting loudly’ are as there. A speech follows, addressed to the Argives.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι ἰόμωροι ἀπειλάων ἀκόρητοι
οὔ θην οἴοισίν γε πόνος τ’ ἔσεται καὶ ὀϊζὺς
ἡμῖν, ἀλλά ποθ’ ὧδε κατακτενέεσθε καὶ ὔμμες.
sentences.l:
“Argives, arrow-dull, insatiate of threats,
surely not alone, at least, will toil and distress
be for us, but some day in this way you will be killed, you also.
sentences.i: “Argives, you dull archers, who cannot have enough of threats, toil and distress will surely not be ours alone; some day you too will be killed in this way.
sentences.n: Acamas answers the Argives’ talk. ἰόμωροι, ‘arrow-dull’, is a rare word, perhaps ἰός ‘arrow’ and μῶρος ‘dull’, and its meaning is not known. ἀπειλάων ἀκόρητοι is ‘insatiate of threats’ (epic genitive plural). οὔ θην is ‘surely not’; οἴοισιν ‘alone’ agrees with ἡμῖν ‘for us’ in the next line, and πόνος … ὀϊζύς are ‘toil’ and ‘distress’. κατακτενέεσθε is an uncontracted future ‘you will be killed’, and ὔμμες is the epic ‘you’ (= ὑμεῖς). ὧδε can also be ‘here’.

sentences.t:
φράζεσθ’ ὡς ὑμῖν Πρόμαχος δεδμημένος εὕδει
ἔγχει ἐμῷ, ἵνα μή τι κασιγνήτοιό γε ποινὴ
δηρὸν ἄτιτος ἔῃ·
sentences.i: Consider how Promachus sleeps for you, overcome by my spear, so that in no way may my brother’s requital go long unpaid;
sentences.n: The point of the boast. φράζεσθ’ is ‘consider’, and ὑμῖν ‘for you’ is a dative of interest: the sight is meant for them. δεδμημένος, ‘subdued’, is the perfect participle of δαμάζω, and εὕδει ‘sleeps’ puts death as sleep. ἔγχει ἐμῷ is ‘by my spear’. ἵνα μή τι … ἔῃ is ‘so that in no way may … be’, with ποινή ‘requital’ unpaid: ἄτιτος is ‘unpaid’ (literally not repaid), and δηρόν ‘long’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 484.

sentences.t:
τὼ καί κέ τις εὔχεται ἀνὴρ
γνωτὸν ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἀρῆς ἀλκτῆρα λιπέσθαι.
sentences.l:
so also any man would pray
a kinsman in the halls, a warder-off of ruin, to leave behind.”
sentences.i: and so any man would pray to leave behind in his halls a kinsman as a defence against ruin.”
sentences.n: Why a brother’s death must be paid for. τὼ is ‘so’, καί is ‘also’, and τις … ἀνήρ is ‘any man’; κε with the present εὔχεται makes it ‘would pray’. γνωτόν ‘kinsman’ is the object of the infinitive λιπέσθαι ‘to leave behind’, with ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ‘in the halls’. ἀρῆς ἀλκτῆρα is ‘a warder-off of ruin’: ἀρή here is ‘ruin, harm’, a different word from ἀρά ‘prayer’. The speech ends here, and the unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀργείοισι δ’ ἄχος γένετ’ εὐξαμένοιο·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and for the Argives grief arose, as he declared it aloud;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and grief came upon the Argives as he declared it aloud;
sentences.n: The Argives’ reaction to the second boast. This is the same line as 458 and 13.417, and takes the same English: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’, ἄχος γένετ’ ‘grief arose’, and the genitive absolute εὐξαμένοιο ‘as he declared it aloud’. It ends at an ano teleia, and the sentence goes on.

sentences.t: Πηνέλεῳ δὲ μάλιστα δαΐφρονι θυμὸν ὄρινεν·
sentences.l: and for Peneleos most of all, wise-minded, it stirred the heart;
sentences.i: and it stirred most of all the heart of Peneleos, wise-hearted as he was;
sentences.n: The grief is felt most by Peneleos. Πηνέλεῳ is the epic dative of Πηνέλεως, and the line runs on from 486 as in 459: μάλιστα ‘most of all’, δαΐφρονι ‘wise-minded’ (‘wise-hearted’ in the idiomatic English; ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ is disputed), θυμὸν ὄρινεν ‘stirred the heart’, with ὄρινεν, the same unaugmented past tense with a movable ν, where 459 has ὄρινε.

sentences.t: ὁρμήθη δ’ Ἀκάμαντος·
sentences.l: And he rushed at Acamas;
sentences.i: and he rushed at Acamas;
sentences.n: Peneleos goes for Acamas. ὁρμήθη is the aorist passive of ὁρμάω, here ‘rushed’, and the genitive Ἀκάμαντος is its target, ‘at Acamas’. The subject is Peneleos, named in the line before. The Greek cuts the sentence at the ano teleia after Ἀκάμαντος, and so does the English.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ οὐχ ὑπέμεινεν ἐρωὴν
Πηνελέωο ἄνακτος·
sentences.l:
and he did not await the rush
of Peneleos the lord;
sentences.i: but Acamas did not withstand the force of lord Peneleos;
sentences.n: Acamas gives way. ὃ δ’ is ‘and he’, now Acamas. ὑπέμεινεν is the aorist of ὑπομένω ‘stand one’s ground against’, with the object ἐρωήν, ‘rush’ (‘force’ in the idiomatic English). Πηνελέωο ἄνακτος is ‘of lord Peneleos’, with the epic genitive -οο and ἄναξ ‘lord’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 489.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ οὔτασεν Ἰλιονῆα
υἱὸν Φόρβαντος πολυμήλου, τόν ῥα μάλιστα
Ἑρμείας Τρώων ἐφίλει καὶ κτῆσιν ὄπασσε·
sentences.i: but Peneleos stabbed Ilioneus, the son of Phorbas, rich in flocks, whom Hermes loved most of all the Trojans, and gave him property.
sentences.n: Peneleos strikes another man. The second ὃ δ’ is Peneleos, the other of the pair. Ἰλιονῆα is the victim, υἱὸν Φόρβαντος πολυμήλου ‘son of Phorbas, rich in flocks’ (πολυμήλου ‘rich in flocks’ as elsewhere). τὸν … μάλιστα Ἑρμείας Τρώων ἐφίλει ‘whom Hermes loved most of the Trojans’ has Τρώων as a partitive genitive. κτῆσιν ὄπασσε is ‘gave property’, ὄπασσε an unaugmented aorist of ὀπάζω ‘give’. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t: τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὸ μήτηρ μοῦνον τέκεν Ἰλιονῆα.
sentences.l: and to him then his mother bore Ilioneus alone.
sentences.i: Ilioneus was the only child his mother bore to Phorbas.
sentences.n: Ilioneus was an only son. τῷ is Phorbas, ‘to him’, and μήτηρ ‘his mother’ is Ilioneus’ mother. μοῦνον Ἰλιονῆα is ‘Ilioneus alone’, so no other child was born to the pair. ὑπὸ … τέκεν is a verb with its prefix split off, the aorist of ‘bear to’, and ἄρ’ is ‘then’. The point of the aside is the loss to his parents, which Peneleos turns to account in his speech.

sentences.t:
τὸν τόθ’ ὑπ’ ὀφρύος οὖτα κατ’ ὀφθαλμοῖο θέμεθλα,
ἐκ δ’ ὦσε γλήνην·
sentences.l:
Him then under the brow he wounded, at the base of the eye,
and pushed out the eyeball;
sentences.i: Peneleos stabbed him then under the brow, at the base of the eye, and pushed the eyeball out;
sentences.n: The blow. τὸν τόθ’ is ‘him then’; ὑπ’ ὀφρύος ‘under the brow’ and κατ’ ὀφθαλμοῖο θέμεθλα ‘at the base of the eye’ are the place, θέμεθλα being foundations or bases. οὖτα ‘wounded’ is the same verb as in 443. ἐκ δ’ ὦσε is ‘pushed out’, with the aorist of ὠθέω, and γλήνη is here the eyeball, the sense of ‘doll’ in 8.164 being another use of the word. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 494.

sentences.t:
δόρυ δ’ ὀφθαλμοῖο διὰ πρὸ
καὶ διὰ ἰνίου ἦλθεν, ὃ δ’ ἕζετο χεῖρε πετάσσας
ἄμφω·
sentences.i: the spear went right through the eye and through the nape, and he sat down, spreading out both his hands.
sentences.n: The spear runs through his head. δόρυ δ’ … ἦλθεν is ‘and the spear went’; ὀφθαλμοῖο διὰ πρὸ is ‘through the eye, on through’, the preverbs standing alone, and καὶ διὰ ἰνίου is ‘and through the nape’. ὃ δ’ ἕζετο is ‘and he sat down’, a past tense of ἕζομαι, a collapse rather than a rest. χεῖρε πετάσσας ἄμφω is ‘spreading both his hands’, with the dual χεῖρε and the aorist participle of πετάννυμι. The unit begins mid-line.

sentences.t:
Πηνέλεως δὲ ἐρυσσάμενος ξίφος ὀξὺ
αὐχένα μέσσον ἔλασσεν, ἀπήραξεν δὲ χαμᾶζε
αὐτῇ σὺν πήληκι κάρη·
sentences.i: Then Peneleos drew his sharp sword and struck him in the middle of the neck, and knocked the head, helmet and all, to the ground;
sentences.n: Peneleos finishes him. ἐρυσσάμενος ξίφος ὀξύ is ‘drawing his sharp sword’, a half-line that recurs word for word. αὐχένα μέσσον ἔλασσεν is ‘struck the neck in the middle’, ἔλασσεν the aorist of ἐλαύνω, and ἀπήραξεν δὲ χαμᾶζε ‘and knocked off to the ground’ the aorist of ἀπαράσσω. αὐτῇ σὺν πήληκι κάρη is ‘the head with its very helmet’. The unit begins after the first word of 496 and ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 498.

sentences.t:
ἔτι δ’ ὄβριμον ἔγχος
ἦεν ἐν ὀφθαλμῷ·
sentences.l:
and still the mighty spear
was in the eye;
sentences.i: and the mighty spear was still in the eye;
sentences.n: The spear is still in the head. ἔτι ‘still’ stresses that the head was severed with the spear still fixed. ὄβριμον ἔγχος is ‘the mighty spear’, the stock phrase, and ἦεν is the epic imperfect of εἰμί, ‘was’. ἐν ὀφθαλμῷ is ‘in the eye’. The unit begins mid-line and ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 499.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ φὴ κώδειαν ἀνασχὼν
πέφραδέ τε Τρώεσσι καὶ εὐχόμενος ἔπος ηὔδα·
sentences.l:
and he, like a poppy-head, held it up
and showed it to the Trojans, and, declaring, spoke a word:
sentences.i: and he held it up like a poppy-head and showed it to the Trojans, and said, declaring aloud:
sentences.n: Peneleos lifts the head. ὃ δὲ is ‘and he’. φή is a rare word for ‘like’, κώδεια is a poppy-head, and ἀνασχών is the aorist participle of ἀνέχω ‘hold up’. The thing held up is not named; it must be the head with the spear in its eye (498–499). πέφραδε is a reduplicated aorist of φράζω, ‘showed’, and εὐχόμενος ἔπος ηὔδα is the stock ‘said, declaring aloud’, the participle meaning ‘declaring’ here.

sentences.t:
εἰπέμεναί μοι Τρῶες ἀγαυοῦ Ἰλιονῆος
πατρὶ φίλῳ καὶ μητρὶ γοήμεναι ἐν μεγάροισιν·
sentences.l:
“Tell, for me, Trojans, of noble Ilioneus
to the dear father and to the mother to sob in the halls;
sentences.i: “Trojans, tell for me the dear father and mother of noble Ilioneus to sob in their halls;
sentences.n: The message Peneleos sends. εἰπέμεναι is an infinitive used as an imperative, ‘tell’; μοι is ‘for me’; Τρῶες is the address. ἀγαυοῦ Ἰλιονῆος is ‘of noble Ilioneus’, and the genitive belongs to both πατρὶ φίλῳ ‘the dear father’ and μητρί ‘mother’, the datives of the people told. γοήμεναι is the epic infinitive of γοάω ‘sob’, and ἐν μεγάροισιν ‘in the halls’ gives the place. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ ἣ Προμάχοιο δάμαρ Ἀλεγηνορίδαο
ἀνδρὶ φίλῳ ἐλθόντι γανύσσεται, ὁππότε κεν δὴ
ἐκ Τροίης σὺν νηυσὶ νεώμεθα κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.i: for the wife of Promachus, the son of Alegenor, will not be glad either at her dear husband’s coming whenever we, the young men of the Achaeans, go home from Troy with our ships.”
sentences.n: Peneleos adds a second house in mourning. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἣ … δάμαρ is ‘for not even she, the wife’ (δάμαρ ‘wife’), and Προμάχοιο … Ἀλεγηνορίδαο is ‘of Promachus, Alegenor’s-son’, the patronymic agreeing with the husband. This is the Boeotian Promachus whom Acamas has just killed: he will not be coming home. ἀνδρὶ φίλῳ ἐλθόντι is ‘at her dear husband’s coming’, a dative of cause; γανύσσεται, ‘will be glad’, is a future. νεώμεθα, ‘we return’, is a subjunctive after ὁππότε κεν. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τοὺς δ’ ἄρα πάντας ὑπὸ τρόμος ἔλλαβε γυῖα,
πάπτηνεν δὲ ἕκαστος ὅπῃ φύγοι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and them then all from beneath a trembling seized, the limbs,
and each looked about where he might flee steep destruction.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and a trembling seized the limbs of them all, and each of them looked about for some way to escape steep destruction.
sentences.n: The effect on the Trojans. ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech. τοὺς δ’ ἄρα πάντας is ‘them all’, and ὑπὸ … ἔλλαβε is ‘seized from beneath’, with the prefix split off; τρόμος ‘trembling’ is the subject, and τοὺς and γυῖα, the people and their limbs, are both in the accusative. The second line is the same as Odyssey 22.43: πάπτηνεν ‘looked about’ is the unaugmented aorist of παπταίνω, and ὅπῃ φύγοι is an indirect question with the optative. ὄλεθρον ‘destruction’ is the object of φύγοι.

sentences.t:
ἔσπετε νῦν μοι Μοῦσαι Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχουσαι
ὅς τις δὴ πρῶτος βροτόεντ’ ἀνδράγρι’ Ἀχαιῶν
ἤρατ’, ἐπεί ῥ’ ἔκλινε μάχην κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος.
sentences.l:
Tell now to me, Muses, who hold the Olympian halls,
who indeed first bloody man-booty of the Achaeans
carried off, when turned the battle the famous earth-shaker.
sentences.i: Tell me now, Muses, you who hold the halls of Olympus, who of the Achaeans was the first to carry off the bloody spoils of men, when the famous earth-shaker turned the battle.
sentences.n: A new invocation, the same as 2.484 and 11.218. In this edition line 508 has no mark of its own and runs straight into the question. ὅς τις δὴ πρῶτος is ‘who indeed first’; Ἀχαιῶν ‘of the Achaeans’ goes with πρῶτος. ἀνδράγρια is a rare word for ‘booty taken from men’ (ἀνήρ and ἄγρα ‘catch’), so ‘man-booty’ in the literal layer, and βροτόεντα ‘bloody’ is its epithet. ἤρατο, ‘carried off’, is the aorist middle of αἴρω. κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος is the stock ‘famous earth-shaker’, Poseidon, and ἔκλινε ‘turned’ the aorist of κλίνω.

sentences.t:
Αἴας ῥα πρῶτος Τελαμώνιος Ὕρτιον οὖτα
Γυρτιάδην Μυσῶν ἡγήτορα καρτεροθύμων·
sentences.l:
Ajax first, Telamonian, wounded Hyrtius,
Gyrtius’-son, leader of the Mysians, strong-hearted;
sentences.i: Telamonian Ajax was first, and stabbed Hyrtius, the son of Gyrtius, leader of the strong-hearted Mysians;
sentences.n: The answer is a list of kills, and the Telamonian Ajax is first. Αἴας ῥα πρῶτος Τελαμώνιος is ‘Ajax then first, Telamonian’, ῥα being ‘then’; Ὕρτιον is the victim, οὖτα ‘wounded’, and Γυρτιάδην ‘Gyrtius’-son’ is a patronymic in apposition. Μυσῶν ἡγήτορα is ‘leader of the Mysians’, an ally of Troy, and καρτεροθύμων ‘strong-hearted’ is the genitive plural of καρτερόθυμος, agreeing with Μυσῶν. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: Φάλκην δ’ Ἀντίλοχος καὶ Μέρμερον ἐξενάριξε·
sentences.l: and Phalces and Mermerus Antilochus despoiled;
sentences.i: Antilochus killed Phalces and Mermerus and stripped them of their armour;
sentences.n: Antilochus’ two kills. Φάλκην and Μέρμερον are the two victims, in the accusative, and the name Ἀντίλοχος follows them. ἐξενάριξε is the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω, which means both kill and strip the armour, so the English says both. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνης δὲ Μόρυν τε καὶ Ἱπποτίωνα κατέκτα,
Τεῦκρος δὲ Προθόωνά τ’ ἐνήρατο καὶ Περιφήτην·
sentences.l:
and Meriones Morys and Hippotion killed,
and Teucer Prothoön slew and Periphetes;
sentences.i: Meriones killed Morys and Hippotion, and Teucer killed Prothoön and Periphetes.
sentences.n: Two more pairs. Μηριόνης δὲ Μόρυν τε καὶ Ἱπποτίωνα κατέκτα is ‘Meriones killed Morys and Hippotion’, with κατέκτα the aorist of κατακτείνω ‘kill’; then Τεῦκρος … ἐνήρατο, ‘Teucer slew’, where ἐνήρατο is the aorist middle of ἐναίρω ‘slay’. The two verbs are told apart in the literal layer. Προθόωνα and Περιφήτην are accusatives, joined by τε … καὶ. The comma at the end of 514 does not close a sentence, and the unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδης δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειθ’ Ὑπερήνορα ποιμένα λαῶν
οὖτα κατὰ λαπάρην, διὰ δ’ ἔντερα χαλκὸς ἄφυσσε
δῃώσας·
sentences.i: Then the son of Atreus stabbed Hyperenor, shepherd of the people, in the flank, and the bronze drew his bowels out through the wound, cutting him down;
sentences.n: The last kill in the list. Ἀτρεΐδης ‘Atreus’-son’ does not say which son of Atreus. Ὑπερήνορα ποιμένα λαῶν is ‘Hyperenor, shepherd of the people’, and οὖτα κατὰ λαπάρην ‘wounded in the flank’ repeats the wound of 447. διὰ δ’ ἔντερα χαλκὸς ἄφυσσε is ‘through, the bowels, the bronze drew out’, with διά an adverb; ἄφυσσε is from ἀφύσσω ‘draw up’. δῃώσας ‘having cut him down’ is the aorist participle of δῃόω. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line 518.

sentences.t:
ψυχὴ δὲ κατ’ οὐταμένην ὠτειλὴν
ἔσσυτ’ ἐπειγομένη, τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε.
sentences.l:
and the soul down through the stabbed wound
rushed, hastening, and darkness covered his two eyes.
sentences.i: and his soul rushed out through the wound he had been given, in haste, and darkness covered his eyes.
sentences.n: Hyperenor dies. ψυχή is the ‘soul’, which leaves the body by the wound: κατ’ οὐταμένην ὠτειλήν is ‘down through the stabbed wound’, οὐταμένην the passive participle of οὐτάω ‘wound by a thrust’. ἔσσυτ’ is the aorist of σεύομαι ‘rush’, and ἐπειγομένη ‘hastening’ is the present participle of ἐπείγομαι. The last clause is the stock death-formula: τὸν δὲ σκότος ὄσσε κάλυψε, ‘and darkness covered his two eyes’. The unit begins mid-line, after the stop.

sentences.t: πλείστους δ’ Αἴας εἷλεν Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς υἱός·
sentences.l: And the most Ajax took, the swift son of Oileus;
sentences.i: But Ajax, the swift son of Oileus, killed the most;
sentences.n: The catalogue ends on the lesser Ajax. πλείστους ‘the most’ is the object, and εἷλεν, ‘took’ in the literal layer, is the aorist of αἱρέω, here ‘killed’. Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς υἱός ‘swift son of Oileus’ makes clear this is the son of Oileus, not Telamon’s son named at 511. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ οἵ τις ὁμοῖος ἐπισπέσθαι ποσὶν ἦεν
ἀνδρῶν τρεσσάντων, ὅτε τε Ζεὺς ἐν φόβον ὄρσῃ.
sentences.l:
for no one was like him at following with his feet
men who had flinched, when Zeus a flight among them rouses.
sentences.i: for none was his equal at pursuing on foot men who had flinched, whenever Zeus rouses flight among them.
sentences.n: Why he killed the most. οὐ γάρ οἵ τις ὁμοῖος is ‘for none was like him’, with ἐπισπέσθαι ποσίν ‘to follow on foot’, the aorist infinitive of ἐφέπομαι. ἀνδρῶν τρεσσάντων is a genitive, ‘of men who had flinched’, the men he pursues, the aorist participle of τρέω. ὅτε τε Ζεὺς ἐν φόβον ὄρσῃ is a general clause, ‘whenever Zeus rouses flight’, with ὄρσῃ the aorist subjunctive of ὄρνυμι and ἐν adverbial, ‘among them’.
